explanations.answer: The Day of the LORD is coming
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The horn sounds because "the Day of the LORD is coming…" and Joel adds that it is near. That is a wake-up call, not a background song. When the alarm goes off for this reason, everybody in the land is supposed to hear it.

explanations.answer: The temple is ready for worship
explanations.explanation: Nothing in these verses says the temple is ready for anything. The alarm is about one thing: the Day of the LORD is coming. A ram's horn here is no ribbon-cutting announcement, friend. It is the kind of sound that makes everybody stop what they're doing.

explanations.answer: A new king is coming to Zion
explanations.explanation: Joel never mentions a new king arriving. The horn is for the Day of the LORD, which is coming and is near. Nobody is rolling out a red carpet here. Joel says to let everyone who dwells in the land tremble.
Joel says the opposite, baker. He calls it "a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness." No sunglasses needed. I'd keep the sunscreen in the cupboard for this one.
Right, it's false. Joel describes "a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness." That is about as far from a beach forecast as you can get. Nobody is planning a picnic for this day.

explanations.answer: There's never been one like it
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Joel says this army is "such as never was of old, nor will ever be in ages to come." Not before, not after. It is the only one of its kind.

explanations.answer: Greater ones are still to come
explanations.explanation: Joel says the reverse of that. This army is "such as never was of old, nor will ever be in ages to come." So he doesn't point ahead to a bigger one. This one stands alone.

explanations.answer: It's just like the armies of old
explanations.explanation: This is the opposite of what Joel says. He describes an army "such as never was of old," so nothing from the past matches it. If somebody tells you it's the usual kind of army, friend, they haven't read verse 2.
Yes, baker. Joel says the land before them is like the Garden of Eden, but behind them it is like a desert wasteland. Lush on the way in, bare on the way out. That's a hard change to look at.

explanations.answer: Like a field ready for harvest
explanations.explanation: Joel describes the reverse. Behind this army the land is like a desert wasteland, and there's no harvest in it. It is the Garden of Eden that shows up in front of them, before the fire and flame get there. A field ready to pick would be a nice thought, friend, but it isn't what the verse says.

No water shows up in this verse, baker. Joel talks about fire devouring in front and flame scorching behind. What's left after that is a desert wasteland. Dry as a cookie sheet left in the oven all night.
That's true, baker. Joel says "surely nothing will escape them." He doesn't say most things or a few things. Nothing.
Joel actually says it, friend. The verse reads "surely nothing will escape them." So this one is true, not false. The way he says it leaves no gap to slip through.
Yes, baker. Joel says "Nations writhe in horror before them; every face turns pale." That's a whole room of people going white at once. Nobody is acting casual.

That's not what Joel describes. The nations writhe in horror, and every face turns pale. Nobody is grabbing their gear and running toward this army. I think I'd be frozen in place too, on my gold base.

explanations.answer: They send gifts to make peace
explanations.explanation: Joel never mentions gifts, friend. What he says is that nations writhe in horror before them. Every face turns pale. Nobody is stopping to wrap anything.
Joel says the opposite, baker. The verse reads "They do not jostle one another; each proceeds in his path." No bumping, no cutting in. Compare that to your average morning commute.
That's the one. Joel says "They do not jostle one another; each proceeds in his path." Every soldier keeps to his own lane. Not an elbow out of place.
You got it, baker. Joel says they climb into houses "entering through windows like thieves." Nobody bothers with the knocker. That's how the army gets inside.
Joel doesn't mention rooftops here. The verse says they climb into houses, entering through windows like thieves. Windows, friend, not the roof.
Joel says it differently. They climb into houses, entering through windows like thieves. Thieves don't ring the doorbell, and neither does this army.
Right, baker. Joel says "The sun and moon grow dark, and the stars lose their brightness." Both lights go dim at once. That's a sky I wouldn't want to look at.

Joel says the opposite, friend. The sun and moon grow dark, and the stars lose their brightness. Nothing is getting brighter in this sky. If you wanted a bigger glow, you'd have to look at my star-filled sky instead.
Joel never says the sun and moon get bigger. He says they grow dark, and the stars lose their brightness. So the change is in the light, not the size. The sky just goes dim.
That's right, baker. Joel says "The LORD raises His voice in the presence of His army." So this is His army and His voice. That changes how you read everything before it.
Joel doesn't name any king of Babylon here. He says "The LORD raises His voice in the presence of His army." The voice belongs to the LORD, friend. No other ruler gets a line in this verse.
Pharaoh, Egypt's king, isn't in this passage at all. Joel says the one who raises His voice is the LORD, in the presence of His army. So this voice isn't coming from any earthly throne. It's His.

explanations.answer: Return to Him with all your heart
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, "Yet even now," and then "return to Me with all your heart…" The word "even now" matters here. The door isn't shut.

explanations.answer: Run to the mountains and hide
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say that. He says to return to Him with all your heart. Hiding isn't in the verse at all. The call is toward Him, friend, not away.

Nothing about building walls shows up in what the LORD says. His word is "return to Me with all your heart." No bricks needed. I've been in tight spots, and I can tell you a taller wall wouldn't have helped me in that drawer either.
Yes, baker. Joel says "So rend your hearts and not your garments…" Rend means tear. The point is the inside, not the show on the outside.

Joel doesn't say altars here. He says to rend your hearts and not your garments. The altar does come up later in verse 17, where the priests weep between the portico and the altar. But the tearing is for the heart, friend.
Joel never talks about tearing fields. The words are "rend your hearts and not your garments." So the tearing is inward. Nobody needs a plow for this one.
That's the reason, baker. Joel says "…He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion." That's why he says to return. It's a God worth coming back to.
Joel says the reverse. He calls the LORD "slow to anger," and also gracious and compassionate. So the reason to return isn't fear of a short fuse. It's who He is.

Joel doesn't describe Him that way. He says the LORD is gracious and compassionate, abounding in loving devotion. And the call is "return to the LORD your God." Nobody is told to go find a faraway place, friend.
That's right, baker. Joel says "And He relents from sending disaster." That's right there in verse 13. It sits in the same breath as gracious and compassionate.
Joel says it plainly, friend. The verse ends "And He relents from sending disaster." So this one is true. It comes right after he calls the LORD gracious and slow to anger.
Yes, baker. Joel says He may "…leave a blessing behind Him…" Notice he says "may" and starts with "Who knows?" So Joel isn't promising it, but he is pointing toward it.

Joel doesn't say a warning here. He says the LORD may turn and relent and leave a blessing behind Him. The warning part already came earlier in the passage, friend. This verse points to what could come after.
Joel says the opposite. He says the LORD may turn and relent and leave a blessing behind Him. Nothing about a curse. That's a very different thing to find behind you.

explanations.answer: A fast and a sacred assembly
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Joel says "consecrate a fast, proclaim a sacred assembly." The horn is calling people together to turn back to the LORD. It's the same horn as verse 1, with a different job.
Joel calls for the reverse. The words are "consecrate a fast, proclaim a sacred assembly." Fasting means going without, friend. It's not a thank-you party.

explanations.answer: A watch on the city walls
explanations.explanation: Nobody is sent to the walls in this verse. Joel says to consecrate a fast and proclaim a sacred assembly. The people are being gathered, not posted as lookouts.

Joel says much more than that, baker. The verse reads "Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the aged, gather the children, even those nursing at the breast." So the call goes out to everyone, not just a few leaders. Even the babies are on the list.

That's right, baker. Joel says "Gather the people," and then names the aged, the children, and even those nursing at the breast. He adds the bridegroom and the bride too. Nobody gets to say it's a meeting for somebody else.
That's the one, baker. The priests are to say "Spare Your people, O LORD…" Joel gives them the words to say. They weep and they ask.
Joel never tells the priests to ask for a king. The words he gives them begin "Spare Your people, O LORD…" So the request is for the people to be spared. That's the whole ask, friend.
Rain isn't in the priests' request. Joel tells them to say, "Spare Your people, O LORD…" So the ask is about the people, not the weather. Nobody is checking the forecast.

Yes, baker. The priests say, "Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’" That's the question they don't want echoing among the nations. They ask the LORD not to let His people become an object of scorn.
Joel doesn't put that question in the priests' mouths. The question is "Where is their God?" So the worry is about what the peoples might say about God's people. Kings don't come up.

Nothing about their numbers shows up in the priests' words. The question they dread is "Where is their God?" That's the one the nations might ask. I don't know about you, friend, but that one would sting.
